title: data-cap: who owns your app's data, and how it may be handled
description: Declare who owns your app's data and how it may be handled. Lint and build checks enforce those rules, and the data documentation regenerates from your code, so it never falls behind. data-cap works next to TanStack Query, Redux or plain fetch, not instead of them.
maturity: data-cap is pre-1.0. Per [VERSIONING.md](https://github.com/maverickcer/data-cap/blob/main/VERSIONING.md), a minor release may still change a Stable API before 1.0, so pin accordingly and read the changelog on every minor upgrade.

hero.heading: Declare who owns your app's data and how it may be handled.
hero.lede: You declare each piece of data once, in a capability: its fields, and the functions that load, change or watch them. `documentData()` adds its `owner` and each field's sensitivity, purpose, legal basis and retention.
hero.support: The ESLint plugin and a build pass check your code against those declarations. The same pass writes the field catalog and ownership report, and the `--check` mode of the script `data-cap init` scaffolds fails CI when a committed copy is stale.
hero.outcome: Lint and build checks enforce those rules, and the data documentation regenerates from your code, so it never falls behind.

install.label: Quick start
install.note: data-cap sits under or next to TanStack Query, Redux, Zustand or plain `fetch` and `useState`. No database, transport or state-library change is needed.

problem.heading: Fetching and state libraries answer different questions.
problem.lede: A fetching library dedupes requests, and a state library gives you a store. Neither says who owns a piece of data or how it may be handled. Neither keeps the page that documents it current.
items: a wiki page about who owns which data
each component's own idea of "loading" and "stale"
a review document that lists where sensitive fields go
problem.conclusion: none of them is checked against the code
problem.closing: data-cap writes those answers down once, in the capability that owns the data. Lint and build checks compare them with the code, and the documentation is generated from it.

model.heading: Full manual control, or batteries included: same primitives.
model.lede: `buildData`, `createDataStore` and a coordinator from `createCoordinator` are the same Stable primitives `createData` composes. Start wherever matches how much control the capability needs.
flow: → Manual path (Stable): `buildData` · `createDataStore` · `createCoordinator`, with full control over execution, retry and caching
→ Batteries-included path (Stable): `createData`, with dedup, per-operation status and an optimistic mutation lifecycle
model.flowDescription: The same Stable primitives can be composed manually for full control, or used through createData for a batteries-included dedup, status, and optimistic-mutation lifecycle.
model.note: Neither path is the one way: pick per capability. Fields are readable from the moment `buildData()` or `createData()` returns. `info` is on every `DataState`, so components never check whether metadata exists.

0 error(s), 2 warning(s), 0 info finding(s):

demo.explanation: A manifest of every active capability, a field catalog, an ownership report and the evidence file, derived statically from the example's code. The warning shows a declared sensitivity and a declared endpoint that disagree; `strictFlow` turns it into an error. CI's examples job compares the README's copy of this output with a fresh run.

guarantees.heading: What it holds to, and where that stops.
guarantees.lede: Each claim states its scope and links to the document that defines it, so you can check the boundary before you rely on it.

items.claim: Ownership is enforced by dropping the write and warning in development, not by throwing.
items.scope: An unowned write is dropped and reported in development, instead of crashing the application. The warning never includes the value (tested for a string value on the `createData` path). data-cap is not an authorization or encryption system.

items.claim: The build tool never executes your code.
items.scope: Discovered files are read through the TypeScript Compiler API and never imported or evaluated. This covers the build tooling only, not your application at runtime.

items.claim: The two-module-system hazard is checked and documented.
items.scope: It applies when a dependency tree loads the package as both ESM and CommonJS, which creates two coordinator instances. A test pins the result: each stays correct, and dedup stops crossing between them.

comparison.eyebrow: Why not TanStack Query, Redux, or manual fetch-and-state?
comparison.heading: You keep all of them.
comparison.lede: data-cap does not replace your transport or your store. It adds one capability per piece of data, naming its owner and how it may be handled, and every component reads it. Lint and build checks compare it with the code.
comparison.caption: Where common approaches stop and data-cap begins
rows: No shared status values, no dedup, no shared optimistic-update rules; every component re-derives its own version
Says nothing about mutation-driven data your app owns outside a query, or how two components agree on ownership
One shared place to put state
Doesn't distinguish declared ownership from incidental access; anything can write anywhere

adoption.heading: From manual control to batteries-included.
adoption.lede: Most applications start with whichever primitive matches how much control a capability needs: full manual control (`buildData`, `createDataStore`, `createCoordinator`) or the batteries-included `createData`. Neither is the one way.
steps: Pick the primitive that fits one capability.
Migrate the next capability when it needs more control or less boilerplate. Each is independent.

notFor.title: You probably don't need it when
notFor.text: Your application is small, one team owns the entire data layer, and there's little reason to separate business capabilities from their storage or fetching implementation. A conventional fetch-and-`useState` pattern, or your existing state-management library alone, may be simpler.

brief.heading: A one-page brief for your manager
brief.oneLine: data-cap records who owns each piece of application data and how it may be handled. Lint and build checks compare that record with the code, and the data documentation is generated from it.
brief.problem: Different parts of an application each work out their own idea of whether data is loading, stale or changed. They disagree, and nobody owns the answer.
brief.whatItDoes: Each piece of data is declared once, with its owner, its fields and how each field may be handled. Checks in the editor and in CI compare the declaration with the code, and the documentation is regenerated from it.
whyItMatters: Who owns each piece of data, and how it may be handled, is written once and checked against the code.
The data documentation is regenerated from the code, and a CI check fails when the committed copy is stale.
It works alongside the fetching and state libraries a team already uses.
brief.whatItCosts: Adopting it means adding the package and declaring one piece of data at a time. It is free, open source software under the MIT licence, and it replaces no existing library.
whatCouldGoWrong: Security fixes target the latest 0.x release only, and there is no long-term-support branch before 1.0.
Ownership is enforced by dropping the write and warning in development, not by throwing. A mistake is reported rather than prevented.
The checks record what the team declared. They do not decide whether a declared purpose or legal basis is lawful.
brief.whatWeAsk: Agree that one feature trials it for a few weeks, then judge from its ownership report whether to extend it.
